The article defines computational functionalism more precisely: it's the assumption that implementing the right kind of computation or information processing is *sufficient* for consciousness to arise — "This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all" [spya-wepmnr]. The reader's phrasing — "the right software could be conscious on any hardware" — captures the substrate-independence implication reasonably well, but it's worth being precise that the core claim is about computation being *sufficient* for consciousness, not just that mind is "what the brain computes."

The second half of the question — why it matters for the whole essay — is where the answer is thin. Seth is explicit that this single assumption is the hinge the entire essay turns on: "if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with" [spya-wepmnr]. All four of his arguments (brains aren't computers, other non-Turing dynamics may matter, life may matter, simulation isn't instantiation) are aimed at undermining this one assumption, and the essay later confirms this structure directly: "Collectively, these arguments make the case that consciousness is very unlikely to simply come along for the ride as AI gets smarter... at least for the silicon-based digital computers we are familiar with" [spya-c5ve5t]. That's the piece to add — the reader has the definition but not yet the stakes of it as the essay's central load-bearing claim.
items.context:
Q: What is 'computational functionalism' and why does it matter for the whole essay?
Reader's answer: It's the idea that the mind is basically what the brain computes, so the right software could be conscious on any hardware.

items.text:
The article's objection is different from this. Seth's argument is that the thought experiment fails at a more basic level: it assumes a biological neuron could be swapped for a silicon one that functions identically, but he argues this is impossible in principle. His example is neurons that fire spikes to clear metabolic waste products — replicating that in silicon "would require inventing a whole new silicon-based metabolism, too, which just isn't the kind of thing silicon is suitable for," so "the only way to seamlessly replace a biological neuron is with another biological neuron" [spya-un9fjn]. He concludes the "argument fails at its first hurdle, given the impossibility of replacing any part of the brain with a perfect silicon equivalent" [spya-ahtr6e].

So the failure isn't an epistemic one about not being able to verify someone's subjective report after the swap — it's that the swap itself can't be done in a way that preserves function, because silicon can't replicate what biological neurons actually do (like metabolic housekeeping). The piece doesn't raise the question of testimony or verification at all in this section; that's a different objection than the one Seth is making here.
items.context:
Q: Why does Seth think the popular 'neural replacement' thought experiment fails to prove consciousness is substrate-independent?
Reader's answer: Because nobody could ever tell whether the person still felt the same after their neurons were swapped — you'd have to take their word for it.

items.text:
The article gives that exact example — "A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet" [spya-npjt4j] — as an illustration of a general principle: a computational simulation of X only instantiates X if X is itself a computational process. Applied to consciousness, this means a simulated brain would only be conscious if consciousness is fundamentally computational, which is exactly the assumption (computational functionalism) that's in question.

So the leap to "can never be conscious" goes further than what this argument alone establishes. Seth is explicit that this is conditional: "will only give rise to consciousness if consciousness is a matter of computation" [spya-pbcr03]. He does think computational functionalism is likely false, based on his other three arguments — but that conclusion comes from those arguments, not from the simulation/instantiation distinction itself, which he presents as a separate, freestanding point that "doesn’t depend on taking account of our cognitive biases" or the other lines of reasoning [spya-nv6tp0].
items.context:
Q: What does Seth mean when he says 'simulation is not instantiation'?
Reader's answer: A simulation of a storm doesn't make anything wet, so a simulated brain can never be conscious.
